name: Tripartism
summary: Tripartism is the arrangement in which governments, employers' organisations and trade unions act as equal social partners in shaping labour and social policy by consultation and negotiation. It is built into the International Labour Organization, whose Declaration of Philadelphia and Convention No. 144 set out cooperation of the three parties, free and independent workers' and employers' organisations, and social-justice aims such as full employment, living wages and social security. The defining sources speak almost only to labour relations, so most statements are null.
scope: The democratic, post-war neo-corporatist form of tripartism as practised in the ILO and in Nordic, Benelux, Austrian, German and Irish social partnership, based on Wikipedia's articles on tripartism, neo-corporatism and social partnership, the ILO's own description of its tripartite structure, and the 1944 Declaration of Philadelphia. It excludes the authoritarian corporatism of fascist states. The sources address labour relations and economic policy; most other statements are low-confidence inferences or neutral because tripartism takes no position on them.

missingStatements.text: Representatives of workers, employers and the government should jointly shape national economic and social policy.
missingStatements.rationale: This is the defining claim of tripartism: the three partners negotiate wages, conditions and policy together.
The Declaration of Philadelphia states this as the first principle on which the ILO and tripartite standard-setting rest.
missingStatements.declined: A slogan whose content is covered by unions-good, regulate-corporations and raise-minimum-wage; not a distinct question.

notes: Later pass 2026-11-14 under rules 7. Every inferred answer from the 2026-10-19 pass was nulled; only positions the ILO's own texts state are kept. Themes searched: the ILO's tripartite structure (How the ILO works, the 2000 General Survey on Conventions No. 144, the 1976 Convention text, the 2026 anniversary article), the Declaration of Philadelphia, and Schmitter's 1974 article on corporatism (saved, but it never uses the word tripartism and was not cited). Government, society, culture, ecology, technology and world themes have no stated position in these sources. Wikipedia (s1, s2, s5) is cited only in superseded earlier versions. The ILO normlex page for C144 and the ILO ACTRAV tripartism page refused access (403), so a University of Oslo copy of the Convention was used. The ILO's own history of tripartism (s9) was added as a defining source.
